listenings.text: People keep asking me what studio year is actually like, so here it is, in order. I get up at five. I have already been in the building for an hour before the first class starts, because the good desks go early. By lunch I have usually thrown away whatever I built the day before. I have not slept a full eight hours since September and I have stopped pretending that is normal. But here is the part nobody tells you: it is not the hours that get you. It is the consistency. Anybody can do one impossible week. Doing an ordinary Tuesday, forty times in a row, at the same standard, is the actual skill, and nobody teaches it to you.

The phrase is burning the candle at both ends, and it is a very old image: you light the top and the bottom, and the candle lasts half as long. I use it with students because it describes the mistake precisely. They protect the middle of the day, which is the part that is already protected by the timetable, and they take the hours off the two ends, which are the only two the body cannot rebuild. Here is what I tell them, and it is never what they expect. I do not ask them to study less. I ask them to decide, in advance, which end they are lighting. Almost nobody has decided. They have just been taking it from both, for months, and calling that discipline.

Every timetable shows you the same thing: hours in, hours out, a gap for lunch. What no timetable shows is the other column, the one nobody writes down. A survey of first-year students this term asked a single question, and the answers were remarkably similar. What have you stopped doing since the year began? Not what have you started — what have you stopped. Sport came first, by a distance. Then seeing people who are not on your course. Then, and this one surprised the researchers, cooking. The point is not that any of this is wrong. Every one of those students made a trade-off on purpose. The point is that almost none of them had ever said it out loud, and a trade-off you have not named is very hard to review.
